opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the very beginning we were in a pretty awkward position. We had the idea that human videos contain an enormous amount of knowledge about how to interact with the world: how a hand approaches a mug, how fingers wrap around a handle, how you open a drawer. But we didn't have a good real robotic arm in the lab, let alone a dexterous hand. So the question became: how do you convince people, and convince yourself, that the model actually learned something useful and not just something that looks nice in a paper figure?

Our approach was to lean heavily on simulation and on the hand itself as the "embodiment." We first extracted human hand poses and object poses from videos, essentially turning a video into a 3D interaction trajectory. Then we asked whether the model could generate new, physically plausible grasps and manipulation motions for objects it had never seen. To check that, we didn't just render the hand. We put the generated hand-object interaction into a physics simulator and tested it: if you apply gravity or perturbations, does the object stay in the hand? Does the hand penetrate the object? Is the contact stable? That gave us a quantitative signal instead of only a visual one.

The second step was retargeting. Even without a physical arm, you can map human hand motion onto a simulated robot hand model, like a Shadow Hand or an Allegro Hand, and see whether the motion still works under that robot's kinematics. If the knowledge only lives in "human hand space," it isn't very useful for robotics. Showing that it transfers across embodiments in simulation was, for us, the key piece of evidence.

Of course, simulation is not the real world, and we knew that. Some reviewers and colleagues were skeptical, and fairly so. But I think the logic held up: if a model can't even work in a well-controlled simulated environment, it has no chance in reality. And if it does work there, with careful physics checks, it's a strong signal that the representation learned from human videos is meaningful. Later, once we had real hardware, a lot of those ideas carried over, and we could close the loop with real-world experiments. In some sense that early constraint forced us to think more carefully about what "learning from humans" really means for a robot.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, that constraint ended up shaping the whole project. We had this model that had learned manipulation priors purely from watching human hands in videos, and the natural thing to do would have been to put it on an arm and show it picking things up. But we didn't have an arm. We had a lab with cameras, a few GPUs, and a lot of students.

So the first thing we did was flip the question around. Instead of asking "what can the robot do," we asked "what does the model actually understand?" And a lot of what it understands you can show without any hardware. You can take a single image of a tabletop scene and have the model predict where a hand would go, how it would orient, what the contact points would be, how the grasp would evolve over the next second or two. We rendered those predictions as trajectories and hand meshes overlaid on the real scene. People could immediately see whether the prediction made sense, because everyone is an expert in how hands grab cups.

The second thing was simulation, but we were careful about it. The temptation is to build a beautiful simulated arm and claim transfer. We knew that would not be convincing to anyone who had actually worked with real robots. So we used simulation mostly as a consistency check. We took the human-derived affordances, retargeted them to a simple gripper, and checked whether the grasps the model proposed were physically stable. That told us the model was not just producing plausible-looking videos, it was encoding something about geometry and contact that held up under physics.

And then the third piece, which I think mattered most, was that we got very explicit about the gap. In the talks and in the paper we drew a line: here is what we have demonstrated, which is a perception and intention model learned from human data; here is what we have not demonstrated, which is closed-loop control on hardware. I think that honesty actually bought us credibility. Later, when collaborators with real arms ran it, the surprising part was how little had to change on the perception side. The hardware specific work was all in the low-level control.

If I'm being candid, not having the arm forced us to make the representation cleaner, because we could not hide weak reasoning behind a flashy video of a robot succeeding once out of twenty tries.

astra-6.text: We didn’t have a real robotic arm, so we had to separate two questions: had the model learned something useful from human videos, and could a physical robot execute it? We focused on the first. The idea was to test in simulation whether the model could use what it had learned to guide a virtual arm through a task. That could demonstrate transfer, but it wouldn’t establish that the system would work on real hardware. That part would still need a physical experiment.
